Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively uses real-time scenes—complete with dialogue, sensory details (the clinking of ice, the turning ceiling fan, the dented surface of the jam), and specific actions—to anchor the emotional core of the story during the narrator's two visits to the mother's house. Between and within these scenes, the author seamlessly weaves exposition and summary to provide vital background on family dynamics (such as the history of the "good chair" and the estranged brother, Gerry) and to efficiently compress the month-long gap when the mother suffers heatstroke, goes through rehab, and returns home. This careful interplay keeps the pacing steady while making the emotional payoffs in the final scene deeply resonant.
